📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mukesh Chhabra, the casting director behind “Dangal” and Shah Rukh Khan‘s upcoming “King,” took aspiring actors and filmmakers behind the scenes of the casting process at a masterclass at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

Industry observers note that the session, “The Casting Magic: Auditions Unplugged,” turned into an extended conversation, with participants asking about everything from self-tapes and social media to age and the demands of the profession. Related Stories Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event.

Introducing Chhabra, festival director Ashutosh Gowariker, whose “Lagaan” was nominated for the foreign-language film Oscar, remarked, “What I like about Mukesh is his eye for character and he will go to any length to find the actors who fit in.”.

Chhabra, whose casting credits include “Dhurandhar,” Aamir Khan’s “Dangal,” Anurag Kashyap’s “Gangs of Wasseypur,” Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana” and “King,” due Dec. 24, described the casting director’s role as a bridge between actors and directors. His work begins with understanding a script and the director’s vision, then determining whether a character calls for an established face or someone upcoming.

It has been revealed that “There is so much talent in our country,” he said. “I send my team all over the country to scout for talent. You have to go to the roots. Our country has so many cultural arts and sub-cultures where so much raw talent is displayed.” Directors, he added, hire him for “my opinion, my ideas, not for my data.”.

Industry observers note that the scale of the search can be considerable. For “Dangal,” he recalled auditioning nearly 14,000 girls over almost two years. For “Gangs of Wasseypur,” he cast 384 people. That film, he noted, “changed my life.”.

Chhabra urged actors preparing for an audition to go beyond memorizing lines and analyze a character’s background, circumstances, social position and motivations. “Designing the scene in your head is important. We want to understand the actor’s intellect. Please do your homework,” he mentioned. “If you understand life, you can understand acting.”.

On self-tapes, his advice was to choose a clean background, ensure good lighting and clear sound, use someone who can deliver cues naturally, and frame the shot close enough to capture the face and eyes. “I want to focus on your face, your performance, not on the painting behind you,” he said.

According to recent reports, asked about social media influencers moving into acting, Chhabra drew a distinction between performing in self-created videos and interpreting a character in a scripted story. “If you really want to take your job seriously, you have to learn the craft,” he said, recommending theater as a way to build confidence and develop an understanding of performance.

It has been revealed that “It’s a part of your life, you’ve got to deal with it. You chose this profession. If you feel rejected and sad all the time, you will miss a lot of opportunities,” he mentioned of rejection.

Industry observers note that “Acting has nothing to do with age, talent is the only thing,” Chhabra stated. He advised performers to keep their appearance simple rather than arrive with a preconceived look for a role.

According to recent reports, he urged actors to stay curious about the world around them. “Read people. Talk to people. Understand people. That’s more important,” he noted. “It is all a game of patience and positivity. If it is meant for you, it will come to you.”.

Industry observers note that questions about nepotism and the casting couch brought some humor into the discussion. Chhabra stated he had rejected several star kids. “Whether you are a star kid or not a star kid, ultimately you have to act,” he said. Asked about the casting couch, he pointed to his seat on stage. “This is the only couch I like. I’m sitting on it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.
  • In a recent development, instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know.

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.

In a recent development, instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

Industry observers note that venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky. Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification.

In a recent development, the bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky.

It has been revealed that spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope.

Industry observers note that check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease.

Want to get a closer look at the planets of the solar system and the stars beyond? Then be sure to check out our roundups of the best telescopes and smart telescopes for observing the night sky.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court mentioned.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they stated she would not confirm her personal information.

In a recent development, several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys remarked their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

Industry observers note that her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also noted to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

Industry observers note that on several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.

Recent findings suggest that ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event.".

In a recent development, "But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he noted.

  • The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Recent findings suggest that latest research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

It has been revealed that "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," states LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

It has been revealed that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Industry observers note that even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising latest questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

According to recent reports, "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred states. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Recent findings suggest that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

Sources indicate that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred notes. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

Sources indicate that by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The newly introduced findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

#219562. Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • The makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

The makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

Industry observers note that it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," said Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Industry observers note that fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves quickly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

In a recent development, "We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," said U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

Sources indicate that the average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," said Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

It has been revealed that though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

It has been revealed that sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She said that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman remarked. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Sources indicate that nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, mentioned BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

It has been revealed that "Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," remarked Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

According to recent reports, "They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," noted Lu.

AlixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," mentioned BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also said she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Recent findings suggest that ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the company mentioned it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

According to recent reports, alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the tech giant is doing well.

In a recent development, "What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," said AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Luc Besson rejects the idea that he reinvented action cinema.
  • “When you don’t have a lot of experience, you have all this freedom.
  • “When Modigliani wanted to paint women with long necks and black eyes, that’s what he did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Luc Besson rejects the idea that he reinvented action cinema. He simply used to have the freedom to experiment.

“When you don’t have a lot of experience, you have all this freedom. You aren’t controlled by major studios and 50 people telling you why you can’t do something because it costs too much. For about 20 years now, people with money have taken control of cinema. They say: ‘I pay, so I decide.’ No. The one who decides is the creator.” Related Stories Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event.

“When Modigliani wanted to paint women with long necks and black eyes, that’s what he did. We need to take this freedom back because we are simply killing art. We’re turning it into something that can be sold, like yogurt or socks. There are four crucial things in the lives of men and women: Water, air, love and art. Without them, we’re dead.”.

He added, “Now, we have replaced everything with money. And it’s going to kill us all.”.

In a recent development, besson was speaking at Torino Film Festival, where he received the Stella delle Mole award for lifetime achievement. Earlier that day, he deadpanned, “I saw the list of all the people who have received it, and I didn’t understand why I hadn’t received it too. I’m not used to receiving awards in my own country, so I’m happy to receive one abroad.”.

Celebrated for “The Massive Blue,” “Léon: The Professional,” “The Fifth Element” and “Lucy,” Besson was honest about his preferences.

Industry observers note that “Some directors are very good at making films about their neighbors – I don’t know how to do that. I like extraordinary stories. I make films to wander, to disappear and explore other worlds. I don’t want to tell the story of my neighbor. I want to tell the story of a guy who drives a taxi in the 23rd century,” he said, referencing Bruce Willis’ role in “The Fifth Element.”.

Sources indicate that “These characters are always a little bit broken by society, always on the margins. Also, I like to explore the strength of women and the weakness of men. If I was asked to make another ‘Terminator,’ I’m not interested. I like Schwarzenegger a lot, but I’d only make that film if the Terminator sat down and mentioned he missed his mom.”.

Besson singled out some of the actors he has enjoyed working with the most, from Gary Oldman to ex-spouse Milla Jovovich and star of “Dogman” Caleb Landry Jones.

“He’s the genius of the decade. He’s a very simple, very sober actor. He doesn’t go out, doesn’t do anything. But when he’s on set, it’s just wonderful. He’ll try everything,” he revealed.

During the presser, Besson said, “If I could make all my films with [Caleb], that would be fantastic.”.

Industry observers note that “As for choosing actors in general, imagine you have to cross the Atlantic in a small boat with just one other person. Choose your partner well, or it will be really hard. Now, I work with actors who are, above all, good people. I don’t want a star surrounded by 15 people.”.

At the moment finishing an animated project that he produced and which will be released next year, Besson continues to collaborate with other directors.

Industry observers note that “If someone else could do it as well or better than me, I don’t need to do it myself. I couldn’t have done ‘Taken’ any better. But ‘The Big Blue’ was different. My parents were divers and I spent 15 years studying dolphins, so I wasn’t going to leave that to anyone else. ‘Dogman’ was the same thing. It was a story I was afraid someone else would ruin,” he recalled.

“Transporter” was another hit for him as a producer.

Industry observers note that “One day, an agent I knew introduced me to a young actor, and I had a drink with Jason Statham. He seemed photogenic. I told him that if I had an idea, I’d call him. I got on a plane and came up with the idea,” he said.

“We wrote it in a month and financed it in three. Louis Leterrier [who directed with Corey Yuen] was an assistant who wanted to start directing. I asked: ‘Are you ready?’ Hollywood doesn’t know how to do it anymore.”.

Recalling his beginnings, he noted, “We were a group of young people who couldn’t get films made because the big studios controlled everything. So we said: ‘Fine, we’ll make them ourselves.’ Suddenly, there were no rules. For 30 years, we did whatever we wanted.”.

According to recent reports, “Unfortunately, it’s getting harder. That’s a real shame because the films haven’t exactly improved, that’s for sure.”.

Reportedly working on a fresh sci-fi project, Besson still advocates the kind of cinema that allows people to escape reality.

In a recent development, “At 14 or 15, I lived far from the city. I could see cows outside of my window, and I felt a strong urge to get away, so I started writing about a taxi pulling up outside my house and taking me off into space. I started writing ‘The Fifth Element’ at 16 because it was my personal way of escaping.”.

“Imagination is a muscle: the more you train it, the stronger it gets. It lets you explore worlds that don’t exist, which is wonderful, because what does exist isn’t that great. Especially right now.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that how did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • Industry observers note that researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that how did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Industry observers note that researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides newly introduced insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

In a recent development, one of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An vital difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

Sources indicate that the results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an notable advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," noted Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

According to recent reports, the discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an vital role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

Upcoming Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

Sources indicate that the team established a newly introduced set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team proposal to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

According to recent reports, A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

According to recent reports, "We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve vital biological functions.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

It has been revealed that jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

Sources indicate that one of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting notable cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

Sources indicate that they found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal notable new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

Recent findings suggest that he added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

In a recent development, gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that he added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

According to recent reports, today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

According to recent reports, south African President Cyril Ramaphosa on Friday attended the launch of French media giant Canal+ Group’s Canal+ Academy at MultiChoice City in Johannesburg. The upcoming pan-African initiative will expand training and professional development opportunities for local aspiring professionals in the creative industries.

According to recent reports, the momentous event — which saw South Africa‘s leader, Canal+ CEO Maxime Saada and other top level executives delivering passionate speeches on the podium — comes after the company’s $2 billion takeover last year of South African pay TV company MultiChoice, which has made Canal+ the dominant player in Africa’s fast-growing pay TV market. Related Stories Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate.

Ramaphosa praised Canal+’s investment in MultiChoice and its decision to make the country an African media market hub, while also lauding the academy as a way to build Africa’s film and TV industry and expand opportunities for young people.

“Today, we are celebrating a significant moment in the country’s broadcasting and creative industries,” Ramaphosa noted, adding: “I am very envious, because in my private life I’ve often said that one day I’d like to produce a movie.”.

It has been revealed that he quipped, “What I’m doing presently, it’s OK. But now, you are living my dream.”.

Sources indicate that south Africa is becoming the first market to introduce the Canal + Academy model. The program, which incorporates the existing MultiChoice Talent Factory, aims to reach between 800 and 1,000 beneficiaries during its first 12 months.

“For Canal+, Africa lies at the very heart of our strategy,” remarked Saada, noting that: “Today, we are a bi-continental group as deeply African as we are European.” He went on to proudly point out that the firm behind “Paddington” is the only entertainment group listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and underlined that “Canal+ Academy is a testament to this faith in Africa.”.

Saada then provided President Ramaphosa and the packed MultiChoice City auditorium a sneak peak of upcoming South Africa-set StudioCanal movie “The Road Home.” Directed by Bill Condon, it stars Cynthia Erivo, South Africa’s Thabo Rametsi (who plays exiled trumpeter Hugh Masekela) and Guy Pearce. The film tells the story of how Paul Simon and numerous South African artists navigated anti-apartheid boycotts to create the Graceland band and one of the bestselling albums — and most politically significant tours — of the 1980s.

The training program will start in 2027 and comprise six year-long courses covering various disciplines across the film, TV, and media value chain, including artificial intelligence and media; digital filmmaking; sports video journalism; acting and the business of African series production.

In an interview with Variety Grace Loubassou, who is sustainability director for Africa at Canal+, noted that: “We have an employability problem here in South Africa, so we are measuring the impact that we can have on that with the academy,” adding that “the real key of our success” will be to see what the program’s up to 1,000 beneficiaries will be able to do concretely in the job market “with the opportunities that we gave them.”.

Industry observers note that loubassou went on to note that she was pleased that South African president Ramaphosa in his speech referred to his recent visit to Silicon Valley and that he is looking to launch a fund to support local artificial intelligence startups in South Africa. “In a lot of revolutions, the African continent was left behind,” she remarked. “So now that there are young people on the continent, half of this population is young and connected. So of course they are able to do an AI stuff,” Loubassou added.

As to how AI is being integrated into the Canal+ Academy program, Loubassou said: “We already have artificial intelligence in our curriculum. So we know it will be the kind of training that people will eager to be in.”.

However she cautioned, “We are fitting it in, but we want to make sure people are using AI for the right reason.”.

Basically “It’s not there to give you creative ideas,” Loubassou explained. “But it’s there to help help you present those ideas and make them more effective.”.

Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry.
  • For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice.
  • Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It promptly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic problems: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing upcoming, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

According to recent reports, in certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

According to recent reports, in addition, it has become significantly more difficult for fresh parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities.".

It has been revealed that protesters on the streets have remarked that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it mentioned that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field.".

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities.".

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

According to recent reports, many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

It has been revealed that for many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

It has been revealed that though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • Industry observers note that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide notable clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

Industry observers note that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Important Clues.

It has been revealed that dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

It has been revealed that "The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan remarked.

In a recent development, "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

It has been revealed that "By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

According to recent reports, to investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

According to recent reports, these findings offer a upcoming perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

According to recent reports, the implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan noted.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a latest era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

Recent findings suggest that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spain and India have moved closer to a fresh film and audiovisual co-production treaty as Spain wrapped its run as Country of Honor at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa and its market, WAVES Film Bazaar.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 21, Marta Serrano, director general of Spain’s Institute of Cinematography and Audiovisual Arts (ICAA), took the Spanish side into a bilateral meeting with India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, whose team was fronted by Prithul Kumar, joint secretary for broadcasting and administration. Representatives of India Cine Hub also joined. The talks pushed forward negotiations on a pact to replace the treaty the two countries signed in 2012. Related Stories Gwyneth Paltrow's 'Goop Guide' Show Coming to Netflix and Spotify, in Which She Explains 'How to Live Goop' in 'All the Ways That Can Be Defined' Skydance Will Need International Films to Supply Theatrical Release Pledge, Raine’s Joe Ravitch Predicts: ‘Those Are Significant Investments’.

Industry observers note that spain Film Commission, the non-profit umbrella group for Spain’s film commissions and film offices, organized the Spanish program in Goa alongside ICAA, which sits under the Ministry of Culture. ICEX–Invest in Spain and Casa de la India provided support. Funding came from the Ministry of Culture and from the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, via its Secretary of State for Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence (SEDIA), under the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan.

“Our participation in IFFI Goa is part of a collaboration strategy that we have been developing with the Indian audiovisual industry for several years. Spain’s recognition as Country of Honor at this edition represents an important milestone, reflecting this collective effort and our close cooperation with ICAA and the other institutions involved. At Spain Film Commission, we will continue to promote these partnerships to create new opportunities for co-production, investment and filming across Spain’s territories,” said Juan Manuel Guimeráns, president of Spain Film Commission.

Sources indicate that the commission and ICAA had backed Spain’s bid for the honor in 2025, and the slot formed part of the Spain–India Dual Year of Culture, Tourism and Artificial Intelligence. Serrano’s team also included Camilo Vázquez, deputy director general for promotion and international relations, and technical adviser Irene López. Spain Film Commission sent general coordinator Lara Molina and communications director Raquel Alonso.

At WAVES Film Bazaar, which ran Nov. 20–24, five production outfits chosen by ICAA – Federation Studios Spain, Pecado Films, Capitán Araña, Acortes Films and ESCAC Studio – pitched their projects and met prospective international partners.

Spanish Day on Nov. 22 featured the panel “Spain: Where Stories Find Their Stage – Incentives, Locations & Co-Production Opportunities,” which made the case for Spain as a shooting destination and co-production partner. Vázquez and Molina were joined by Usha Jadhav of Acortes Films, Miguel Fabián Salazar of ICEX and Guillermo Rodríguez of Casa de la India. Spain Film Commission pointed to the country’s tax incentives, range of locations, crews and production facilities, plus the support its countrywide network gives visiting shoots. The session also showcased five Spanish projects seeking Indian partners, among them “The Dragon Letter,” Ladakh-born director Stanzin Jigmet’s project based on his Student Academy Award-winning short of the same name, and “Serendipia,” an India-Mexico-Spain romance.

According to recent reports, the commission also helped run a Spanish Networking Night that drew more than 200 guests. Among them were Indian ministry officials Prabhat, additional secretary; Kumar; and K.K. Nirala, joint secretary for institutions.

On the festival side, IFFI’s Spanish selection included the world premiere of Juana Macías’ “Looking for Michael” (“Persiguiendo a Michael”), Pedro Almodóvar’s “Amarga Navidad,” Jaime Lorente’s “El mal hijo” and “Trinidad,” from Laura Alvea and José Ortuño.

It has been revealed that the delegation also attended screenings of Anna Saura’s documentary “Carlos Saura. Ese niño de la fotografía” and “Mudras. Bailando hilos invisibles,” directed by María Salgado Gispert and produced by Anna Saura, Marino García and Bobby Bedi. That film is the first official co-production between the two countries under the 2012 treaty.

The Goa push comes as Spain Film Commission, founded in 2001, marks its 25th anniversary.

Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".
  • In a recent development, he should know.
  • Akerson stated Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".

In a recent development, he should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson stated Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

It has been revealed that "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a massive change.".

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable.".

His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, mentioned selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

It has been revealed that "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has mentioned several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

Industry observers note that GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the tech giant's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates.".

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he stated.

Akerson remarked he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

According to recent reports, akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson remarked. "She's done a terrific job.".

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

It has been revealed that "This is vital. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.
