📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”.

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

Recent findings suggest that during the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul proposal began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their fresh mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s prepares planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

It has been revealed that “We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he stated.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters.

Industry observers note that fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

Sources indicate that they’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov stated. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”.

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

Sources indicate that but despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu noted he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”.

It has been revealed that in his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had remarked the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government looks. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”.

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov stated.

Merritt R. Turetsky Profile (2026).

Boglands are formed by waterlogged conditions and a lack of oxygen that slows down plant decomposition, causing organic matter to accumulate as a thick layer of peat. Peatlands occupy only 3% of the planet’s land area, but store about 30% of soil carbon. “In this liminal space, where land is water and water is land,” writes ecologist Merritt Turetsky, “a strange and haunting loveliness reveals itself.” This is not obvious to most people, who often laugh when told that she studies bogs. Such sceptics will be won over by her fascinating book.

Leah C. Stokes MIT Press (2026).

Sources indicate that at university, environmentalist Leah Stokes was stirred by the 2006 documentary An Inconvenient Truth, which argued that each of us is responsible for reducing global warming. Only later, as an associate professor in California, did she realize that the chief culprit is fossil-fuel infrastructure. In 2022, Stokes had a major role in pushing the US government to pass landmark legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act, with more than US$400 billion in climate investments. Her absorbing book unpacks “the blow-by-blows of how this climate law was made”.

Sources indicate that james K. Galbraith Univ. Chicago Press (2026).

Industry observers note that veteran economist James Galbraith begins his striking attack on mainstream economics in the United States by declaring that his academic discipline has long been a “fraud”. For decades, economists have embraced the idea that “power over money should be kept far from democratic politics”. And yet, oligarchs from finance, technology, pharmaceuticals and several other fields now hold political power. Economists, he argues, continue to deploy outdated tools from a century ago, which are weakening democracy.

Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today.
  • According to recent reports, two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation.
  • Industry observers note that scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A newly introduced scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

According to recent reports, two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline.

Industry observers note that scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

The researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

According to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

Industry observers note that under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together.

It has been revealed that despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

Another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

According to recent reports, the researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

When additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

It has been revealed that as a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago.

Industry observers note that the spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

The first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

As atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more vital. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

Even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life.

These findings also offer a fresh perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

When Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made new environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Sources indicate that rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

Industry observers note that the researchers acknowledge that notable uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an important role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham‘s office has spoken out against an upcoming Channel 4 documentary featuring an interview with disgraced former BBC presenter Huw Edwards.

Industry observers note that announced on Thursday, the doc sees Edwards — who, in 2024, was convicted of three counts of making indecent images of children and given a six-month suspended sentence — speak publicly about his downfall and criminal actions for the first time. Titled “Huw Edwards — Guilty,” it’s set to air on Channel 4 Dec. 1. Related Stories Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event Beyoncé Makes Grammys History as First Artist With 100 Nominations.

The doc has stirred up quite a bit of backlash in the U.K., with several members of Parliament speaking out against it, and now Burnham has added his voice to the mix. In a statement to BBC News, an official spokesperson mentioned: “Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say.”.

The spokesperson added that these “are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions” and said that broadcasters “are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions.”.

Asked if the prime minister believed Channel 4 has not acted responsibly by making the documentary, the spokesperson said: “Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them.”.

In a recent development, representatives for Channel 4 did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment. The broadcaster told the BBC yesterday that the documentary’s director, Patrick Forbes, is “highly experienced” and there were “no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall.”.

A game Justin Timberlake gave a welcome reminder of his varied talents on The Tonight Show on Thursday night, variously dressing up as a “sexy” turkey, doing a spirited Scottish accent and of course dancing and singing like only he can.

In what felt like a throwback to the innocence and goofiness of the Obama years, Timberlake was on top form, taking part in sketches, dance bits and sitting down for an interview to promote the 20th anniversary of his classic album FutureSex/LoveSounds and the four-part documentary series Timberlake that begins streaming on Apple TV on Dec. 11. Related Stories TV Justin Timberlake Documentary Trailer: "He's Not Who I Thought He Was" Music Justin Timberlake Teases New Music: "I've Been Chef-ing".

With the Roots backing them up, Fallon opened the show with Timberlake for a song and dance number, with the duo going through The History of Party Songs. In a segment that is catnip for 90s kids, the tracks covered included Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body” and more.

Industry observers note that in the interview section, Timberlake opened up about the making of FutureSex/LoveSounds, reminding the audience that that his influences on the album included “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics and INXS.” He stated that on the song “SexyBack” he was channeling Bowie doing “Rebel Rebel” and he had to fight the recording tech giant on the production. “They fought me on it. Well, I brought it in and it was like, ‘It’s too fast.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.’ … [And they said], ‘You don’t sound like you, your signature falsetto.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.'”.

Sources indicate that on the infamous lyrics to “SexyBack”, Timberlake added, “That song does not make any sense. I’ve mentioned this. It makes zero sense. But, it’s why it makes sense.”.

In a particularly poignant part of the interview, Timberlake discussed his love for and influence of the late D’Angelo, describing him as “my guy.” “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything. You know, he was one of those artists… rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”.

On why he decided to take part in the Apple docuseries — which Fallon said tackled Timberlake’s career highpoints and personal low points — the Grammy-winner said that initially he “was really reluctant to do it” agreeing with Fallon that he was “sort of famously private.” His relationship with director Fisher Stevens softened his stance and that the doc he has “mustered up some courage to talk about some things that I’ve never talked about before, that, you know, things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”.

Sources indicate that timberlake mentioned he found the doc experience “cathartic” and he hoped it would help others to share their troubles. “Everybody’s going through something. And I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like have made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.”.

According to recent reports, in the recent past, Timberlake has had a number of public incidents including being arrested for DWI in the Hamptons in June 2024 and revealing in July 2025 that he was diagnosed with Lyme disease. There was also the cheating rumors in 2019, and subsequent public ridicule, after the singer was caught holding hands with co-star Alisha Wainwright during the filming of Palmer. Timberlake had to glitch a public apology about the Palmer incident on Instagram, calling it a “strong lapse in judgment.”.

In a recent development, one sketch that’s likely to get a lot of play on social media was “Sexy Butterball Hotline,” where Fallon (Rocky Drumstick) and Timberlake (Pecker Spatchcock) played two very sexy turkeys — “the dirtiest birds in the coop” no less — manning an after dark Thanksgiving helpline. A sample of some of the lines from Rocky and Pecker in this bit: “Who says the turkey can’t be the one who does the stuffing?” “Is it Black Friday? ‘Cause my clothes are 100% off.” “I can’t wait till you lay me down on the table right in front of Grandma.” Good clean fun.

#219519. Latest Update: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)

Latest Update: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed.
  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a latest top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.
  • In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

According to recent reports, U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a latest top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It has been revealed that it's part of airlines' substantial bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more key as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," noted Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt remarked.

According to recent reports, "People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he mentioned. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that its upcoming cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

According to recent reports, american Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

Sources indicate that "You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, remarked in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

In a recent development, first class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American stated. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

Sources indicate that "It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt remarked. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

In a recent development, there are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline claims.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter remarked last month.

#219518. Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Major Bang.
  • An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history.
  • Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Major Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so promptly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

In a recent development, the discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Recent findings suggest that gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe.

Sources indicate that during the first billion years after the Major Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

In a recent development, as galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

One reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Significant, Too Fast.

According to recent reports, nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

In a recent development, the black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

According to recent reports, astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Massive Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

In a recent development, "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," states Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.".

In a recent development, the pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.".

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1].

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair.

According to recent reports, the discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

It has been revealed that obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

Fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," notes Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2].

A Upcoming Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies.

In a recent development, exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

Industry observers note that "Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," states Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.".

Tyson Fury does not have schizophrenia, despite revelations made in the promo for his upcoming Netflix feature doc. These revelations have now been removed from the film.

In the trailer for “Tyson Fury,” the British boxing champion is seen discussing his mental health struggles, noting that when quizzed by a psychiatrist he “ticked all the boxes … depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder…” Fury’s wife then adds that he’s a “mild schizophrenic.” Related Stories Beyoncé Makes Grammys History as First Artist With 100 Nominations Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate.

The comments sparked numerous headlines and also prompted British boxing regulators to look into the matter to ensure that Tyson would be medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in their long-awaited bout due to take place Dec. 11. But now Paris Fury has walked back those claims, putting out a statement denying that her husband has schizophrenia. Netflix has subsequently edited the scene in question out of the documentary.

In a recent development, “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” Paris Fury said. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic’. While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.”.

Added a Netflix spokesperson: “Following newly introduced information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to patch the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.”.

Now showing on Netflix and directed by Lucy Wilcox, “Tyson Fury” charts the triumphs and setbacks of the heavyweight champion’s career, his struggles with mental health and addiction, the loss of a child, complex family relationships and the question of what it means to be a man.

The film was produced by Optomen, part of Banijay Entertainment, which also produced Netflix’s “At Home With the Furys” reality show featuring the boxer and his family, now onto its third season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, british actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year. With roles in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation and the recently released Ebenezer, he’s been busy crafting new interpretations of well-known characters.

“To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year.

Sources indicate that the 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K. after over a month of press for Carrie and Ebenezer and a stint in Portland, Oregon. “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind, but it’s been very enjoyable,” he claims. After a breakout performance in 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, 2026 has been the actor’s biggest year to date between the two projects and a role in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Related Stories TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up.

According to recent reports, with Carrie, Conti stepped into the role of teen bully Billy Nolan, first played on screen by John Travolta in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Conti had read Stephen King’s novel but hadn’t seen De Palma’s film, which he stayed away from during filming. Conti’s Billy, while still one of the villains of the story, is different from Travolta’s take on the character. “I was worried that even inadvertently or subconsciously I would copy things about that performance, and I really wanted it to be all my own,” he states.

In a recent development, ebenezer finds Conti stepping into the shoes of the titular character of Ebenezer Scrooge — well, the younger version of him anyway. The actor heard that Ti West would be making the film, and as a big fan, he sent in a self-tape. Much like with Carrie, he tried not to take too much inspiration from previous versions of the story, but there’s one adaptation that stands out.

“[The Muppets version] is probably the best one. I mean, it’s amazing, that film. Michael Caine gives such a genuinely brilliant, dramatic performance in that film against the Muppets,” he claims. “He takes it so seriously, and that is the beauty of that film is that you’d think he was talking to John Gielgud, and he’s talking to Fozzy.”.

Despite The Muppets Christmas Carol being his main experience with the story beforehand, he did watch the 1951 film adaptation starring Alastair Sim as Scrooge. “I really liked,” he notes.

Below, the actor digs into his last year in roles, what he’s looking to do next and how he’d spend a perfect day in London.

I’m always curious, as someone who enjoys it — have you seen Carrie: The Musical?

It has been revealed that we watched it. We saw a theater production on Granville Island in Vancouver. It was a youth theater production of Carrie: The Musical. [The cast of Carrie] all went to go and see it. Mike [Flanagan] actually put the cast of that production of Carrie in the show. They’re all at the prom. Throughout the show, they’re in the background at the school, which was really, really fun.

Recent findings suggest that how has the year been? You were busy with Carrie and now Ebenezer.

Industry observers note that [Carrie] was my first substantial press tour. It was my first time doing a press junket and all of these things. It feels like the biggest thing that I’ve done so far [with] how much I’ve been promoting it. It was all incredibly exciting. [In Carrie,] I’m playing another character that has several sides to him, after [I did in] Beetlejuice. It’s another deceptively charming, manipulative character, which is interesting that I keep taking. (Laughs).

Where do you think that’s coming from?

In a recent development, something about me, I don’t know. Something untrustworthy. Honestly, it is a treat to play characters like that because you get the chance to do multiple things at once, present a character that has many layers and is complex and isn’t wholly one thing or another. It was a great role. It was a really meaty role to sink my teeth into, and it was an honor to play a character of that literary significance. It was a privilege to be entrusted with that.

As an actor, are you drawn to characters that are different from you, then?

Industry observers note that it’s nice to get outside of yourself — that’s part of the fun of it. Growing up, the films I was watching, I was a lot more drawn to flawed or strange or darker characters. I grew up watching Steve Buchemi in Fargo and Philip Seymour Hoffman in Punch-Drunk Love and Talented Mr. Ripley. Those are the kind of characters that I always really loved to watch.

The scope of the projects you had this year has been quite large. Are you drawn to that or looking to change it?

You’re right. They are quite large-scale. I think I’m drawn to things that are a little out there and a little strange. Horror is one of the best genres to explore that area because it emboldens filmmakers to experiment and take risks and be a bit weird and a bit dreamlike. That’s why I gravitate towards horror a lot, and it’s probably what I watch the most of in the cinema.

Is that where you got your love for it? Were you big into horror as a kid?

I think so. It’s not horror, just things that are a little strange. My mom brought me up on Charlie Kaufman films. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is my mom’s favorite film, so I watched that quite early. Things that tap into that dreaminess and that weirdness and spookiness — that’s up my alley. But it would be a dream to do a Before Sunrise kind of thing, where it’s just two people talking for an hour and a half. I would love to do something like that next.

Is that what you’re looking to do going forward then?

It has been revealed that it could be anything. I really want to leave myself open. I would love to do something a little more scaled down, kind of dialogue-heavy thing. I could never have imagined the caliber of director and the caliber of actor that I’ve been working with. If I can only just continue to do that, I will be very lucky indeed. I’ve gotten to work with some of my absolute heroes, and that’s been wonderful. But I want to keep working in horror as well. Horror’s having a really exciting moment right now, especially young people in horror, with Obsession and Backrooms. I will stay as long as it’ll have me. Horror, fantasy — that’s what I grew up with, and I want to explore that more as well.

What does your ideal day off look like?

In a recent development, I would wake up at 10:30 a.m.-ish. I’m a very late-to-bed, late-to-rise kind of person in my free time. I’d wake up then; I’d get a coffee; I’d go for a walk. I have to do 10,000 steps a day. I’m like a dog. I have to be walked. Then I would go and see a movie. I would go to the cinema. I would probably go to the Prince Charles Cinema, which is my favorite in the world. I don’t know whether I’d see it on my own or with somebody else. I do go on my own to the cinema a lot. That’s one of my favorite ways to watch a film. Then I’d get a nice dinner. I might go shopping a little bit. I might go record shopping, go DVD shopping. Then I would go to the pub maybe, and then I would go to bed at 1 a.m. I’m being very specific with the times.

I’m unfamiliar with Prince Charles Cinema; why is that your favorite theater?

Just the vibe there, and the programming. There’s always something on there that’s worth seeing. I honestly have so much to thank that cinema for because the education in film that it has given me is just insane. I’ve seen so many films there for the first time. It’s one of the few places, in London especially, where you can see old films and cult films and things that don’t get screened very often. You can go and experience them in the theater, and that’s a very valuable thing. They were going to possibly get shut down, but they’ve just won the battle against the landlord or whatever. They’re going to be there for another 25 years. I’m very happy about that.

This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a big impression on scientists.
  • According to recent reports, the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes.
  • According to recent reports, many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a big impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

According to recent reports, the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report.".

According to recent reports, many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," mentioned corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

According to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground.

Visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

According to recent reports, female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

In a recent development, when an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome.

The spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

Industry observers note that however, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

Industry observers note that the research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond mentioned.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

Not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders.

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an vital role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

In a recent development, trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

Recent findings suggest that "We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond remarked. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.".

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

This restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond stated.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to New Medicines.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing new ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond mentioned.

It has been revealed that the study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.
  • According to recent reports, that isn't a random comparison.
  • A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

According to recent reports, that isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

"The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University remarked in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events.".

The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy, a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.

Recent findings suggest that responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years,.

In a recent development, they determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits.

In a recent development, "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar stated. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years.".

An important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star.

In a recent development, when Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025.

Sources indicate that one of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Significant Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier.

This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass.

"It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Substantial and Little Bao," Karambelkar said. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries.".

Industry observers note that the team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #219510. Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
  • Sources indicate that researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown.
  • Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and showed no further changes in brightness.

Sources indicate that researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object.

Industry observers note that researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

In a recent development, the third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Significant Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue.

The unusually short duration of the brightening provides an important clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

Industry observers note that phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

According to recent reports, to investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

The results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Big Bang.

It has been revealed that for roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

#219509. Tech Report: The British Government is Turning Everyone Into a Prepper

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1840 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The British Government is Turning Everyone Into a Prepper

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in 2010, the UK experienced one of its coldest ever winters, with heavy snowfall bringing major roads to a standstill.
  • It has been revealed that next time, Brian decided, he would be prepared.
  • Preppers generally operate on the fringe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 2010, the UK experienced one of its coldest ever winters, with heavy snowfall bringing major roads to a standstill. Brian, an engineer in central Scotland, had little food in the house. He donned a backpack, took one of his children’s sledges, and trudged a mile and half to queue outside the nearest supermarket. Shelves were emptying, and tempers were fraying.

It has been revealed that next time, Brian decided, he would be prepared. “It’s very hard to look your kids in the eye when you’re looking at a relatively empty cupboard,” he says. Brian started building up a store of non-perishable food and other supplies, ready for unexpected shortages. He’s now part of the UK’s prepper community—a group of survivalists who plan proactively for emergency situations such as natural disasters or infrastructure breakdowns. He shares his tips on YouTube as Scottishprepper73; he reckons his family could live a full year off his stash.

Preppers generally operate on the fringe. They’re used to people considering them crazy and paranoid. When Brian tells friends about his plans, they often respond with jokes. Or worse, they tell him “I’ll just come to your house.” Then, last month, the UK government released its “Be Ready” campaign, which advised households to stock up on three days’ worth of bottled water, tinned food, and other essentials. The advice, the Cabinet Office stated, was “the first stage of a three-year campaign to help households across the UK feel better prepared for events such as severe weather, which can occasionally affect services including power, water, phones and the internet.”.

Prepping was flung into the mainstream, and British preppers—a minority in a largely US-dominated scene—have found themselves drawn out of their (metaphorical) bunkers and into the limelight.

For the most part, preppers I spoke to welcomed the government advice, though they unanimously felt it didn't go far enough (“What’s your strategy for day four?” Mike Chappell, a Greater Manchester-based prepper, says.) But public reactions, they say, have been mixed.

In a recent development, dan Goss, who is based in Liverpool and runs the Start Prepping UK website, states traffic to his site “went bananas,” reaching around 50,000 visitors at one point. The news, he says, has “broken people’s normalcy bias,” legitimising the idea of prepping in a way that no amount of bleak climate news can. He’s observed a rise in what he calls the “normal person prepper”—people who aren’t interested in planning for an apocalypse or learning advanced survival skills, but want to build basic household resilience. Glyn Smith, founder of the prepper community UK Survival Network, reports a similar spike in interest. “It’s not lone survivalists; it’s mums, dads, couples, and retirees,” he says. “Normal people who want practical peace of mind.”.

Dan recommends: In terms of hardware or capabilities it’s hard to beat a Sawyer Mini water filter. They’re tiny, lightweight, need no energy source to run, and can filter something like 100,000 liters of water before they need to be replaced.

According to recent reports, there’s also been pushback. Every time prepping hits the news, Brian says, some people respond with aggression. When he’s spoken to media before, multiple people have made death threats. “‘I’m not going to waste money on preps, I’ll just buy a shotgun and come to your house,’ yada yada,” he says. For this reason, he, and several other preppers I spoke to, asked to be identified only by their first name. As well as hostility, Goss says, some people complain that they can’t afford to prep, or that the government should provide. A common sentiment, Chappell says, is that “nothing ever happens anyway.” Some accuse preppers of fearmongering.

It has been revealed that the general image of the prepping community probably doesn’t help. Think “prepper” and you might imagine a caricature of a man in camo and armed to the teeth, either hunkering down in a nuclear bunker or camping out in the wilderness. But the preppers I speak to present a much more mundane, inclusive, and, well, British approach to prepping. They are keen to distance themselves from the idea of the “doomsday prepper.” Instead, they prep for less extreme but more likely incidents. As the UK anticipates winter weather buffeted by an El Niño climate pattern, they worry about storms, floods, and crop failures. Something as simple as a burst water pipe or power cut could cause localized chaos. Then there’s the threat of cyberattacks: Just this month, supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe were hacked in an attack France believes was conducted by Iran.

Glyn recommends: A Lifesaver bottle or Lifesaver Jerrycan and an EcoFlow power station such as the Delta 3.

In a recent development, regardless, states Ana, a prepper based in south Wales, the impacts are likely to be the same. “It’s going to be affecting potentially your food supply in the supermarkets, your water, your electricity,” she says. Ana has a food channel on YouTube, but pivoted to prepper content when she realized most people had no idea how to preserve food for long-term storage. She grew up growing food, cooking from scratch, and keeping a full pantry, and has maintained these habits. The Covid-19 pandemic reminded her just how vulnerable the UK supply chain is. She was pregnant at the time and noticed a shortage of baby formula; a supermarket worker told her people had been buying it to put in their coffee and tea.

It’s always a good idea to keep a store of basics like bottled water and long-life food. True preppers often invest in more specialized items. Brian gives me a virtual tour of the shed where he stores his supplies, neatly arranged in floor-to-ceiling shelving units. He points to different types of water filtration kits, including a LifeSaver Jerrycan capable of purifying up to 20,000 liters, and rattles off medical supplies (“Antibiotics, tourniquets, chest seals, splints”). He has a few different cooking setups, such as foldable stoves that use gas canisters, and keeps buckets of freeze-dried food that will last for 25 years. Next door, he tells me, there are 165 gallons of fresh water that he refreshes every six months.

Brian recommends: A reasonably sized power bank such as a Bluetti Elite 300, which will give you days of backup power for your home. Add in some solar panels and you have a two-to-three-year renewable power source.

Many preppers prepare to go off-grid if the power and internet fail, but Brian has staked his bets on a tech-heavy setup. He has a generator, his house is fitted out with solar panels, and he uses an air source heat pump for heating. He has a backup heater that runs on diesel, and several extremely powerful portable power stations (think a rechargeable power bank, but with enough capacity to keep appliances like a microwave going). He uses Starlink for internet access and runs two different mesh networking systems, with high-frequency radio acting as his ultimate fallback. In his shed, he has plenty of torches, lanterns, candles, radios, walkie-talkies, and a night-vision headset. The way he sees it, you might be able to survive without power, but it wouldn’t be much fun. “We’ve got enough tech these days that life doesn’t have to be uncomfortable,” Brian notes.

This is a key difference between the US and UK prepper scenes: While many US preppers proposal to “bug out” and live alone off-grid, British preppers mainly plan to stay at home. “We don’t have that vast wilderness to escape to,” indicates Chappell, who makes content as the UK Urban Prepper and keeps most of his at-home supplies stacked in what used to be the dining room. When we speak, Chappell has a four-week-old daughter, so his stocks include enough formula milk to get her to solid foods. Nappies are too bulky to stockpile en masse, but he has enough for a short-term concern and a fallback of old-fashioned terry towel nappies.

According to recent reports, mike recommends: My number one would be any kind of water filter. I love the Grayl one for simplicity.

According to recent reports, while prepping is often depicted as a lone wolf activity, British preppers are, on the whole, more community-minded. The scene in general has a degree of secrecy around it; some preppers keep their preps tightly under wraps out of fears that, if people know what they have, they could become a target.

It has been revealed that goss dismisses fears of people turning on each other in a crisis. He evokes a sense of Blitz spirit: when times get tough, he suggests, people tend to come together rather than pull apart. In any case, he doesn’t really have a choice. Like Chappell, he lives in a terraced house in an urban area—a far shout from a private bunker. “Like it or not, you’re going to wind up working with your neighbors during a significant giant blackout event or something,” he notes. “And it would be a really good idea for you to kind of plan for that ahead of time.” He suggests gaining trust by setting up a street WhatsApp group and doing small favors for neighbors. In an emergency scenario, pooling resources and knowledge may be more effective than going it alone. And if things did descend into looting and fighting–well, wouldn’t you want your neighbors on side?

Recent findings suggest that ana recommends: A power station like Allpowers’ R1500, an Aferiy 2400w station, or the Ecoworthy PS2400. All have great capacity and multiple charging options.

In a recent development, others thought this view might be too optimistic. “When you’re bombarded with information 24/7 and you’re deprived of any information in a general power cut, it wouldn’t take long before people get nervous and start to do stupid things because they panic,” Brian indicates. “You get a fear response. Fear leads to poor choices, potentially fatal ones.” He’s thought about what he’d do if friends really did turn up on his doorstep like they joke about. “It’s a difficult one,” he says. “I don’t have an answer.”.

Recent findings suggest that in that kind of scenario, Chappell has a plan to bug out, but just to a family member’s home. His house is surrounded by people he doesn’t know, and he can’t predict how they might react. It’s not that he doesn’t want to help people, he claims, but he’s not willing to risk his family’s safety.

According to recent reports, of course, these plans go well beyond a three-day water-and-beans buffer. For many of the people I speak to, prepping is also a hobby. There are meet-ups and workshops. Goss indicates he enjoys camping and tending his allotment—activities that fit neatly into the prepper skillset (he’s also into archery, just to complete the image). But still, it’s nice to be ready, just in case. “This is not a way of life where I sit in a bunker hoping for the sky to fall. I want nothing ever to happen,” Chappell says. “But it’s insurance, right?”.
